exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Jacobian Determinant of a Transformation

question.text:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 3u+2v \\u+3v\end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) =3u+2v $ and $y(u,v) = u+3v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &=3 & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= 2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= 1 & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 3 \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1& 3 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 9-2 \\[5pt] &= 7. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}\left( \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \right) =\begin{bmatrix} e^{u+v}\\ \ln(uv)\end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) = e^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v) = \ln(uv).$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &=e^{u+v} & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= e^{u+v} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= \dfrac{1}{u} & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= \dfrac{1}{v} \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} e^{u+v} &e^{u+v} \\ \dfrac{1}{u} & \dfrac{1}{v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=e^{u+v}\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{v}\right) -e^{u+v}\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{u}\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{u+v}}{v}-\dfrac{e^{u+v}}{u}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{u+v}(u-v)}{vu}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} u^2-v^2\\ u^2+v^2 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) = u^2-v^2$ and $y(u,v) = u^2+v^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &= 2u & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= -2v \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &=2u & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 2v \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} 2u & -2v\\ 2u& 2v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=2u \cdot 2v - (-2v) \cdot 2u \\[5pt] &= 4uv+4uv\\[5pt] &=8uv. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}\left( \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \right) = \begin{bmatrix} e^ {u+v} \\ u^2+v^2 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x=e^{u+v}$ and $y=u^2+v^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &=e^{u+v} & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= e^{u+v}\\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= 2u & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 2v \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} e^{u+v} &e^{u+v}\\ \quad\ 2u \quad & \quad\ 2v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=e^{u+v} \cdot 2v - e^{u+v} \cdot 2u \\[5pt] &=2e^{u+v}(v-u). \end{align*}

question.text:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} ue^{\large v}\\u+v^2 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) = ue^{\large v}$ and $y(u,v) = u+v^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &= e^{\large v} & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= ue^{\large v} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= 1 & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 2{v} \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix} e^{\large v} & ue^{\large v}\\ 1 & 2v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 2ve^{\large v}-ue^{\large v}\\[5pt] &= e^{\large v}(2v-u). \end{align*}

question.text:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 3u^2+2v\\u+2v^2 \end{bmatrix}. \] compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1\\1 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) = 3u^2+2v$ and $y(u,v) = u+2v^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &= 6u & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= 2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= 1 & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 4{v} \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} 6u & 2 \\ 1& 4v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 6u \cdot 4v -2 \cdot 1\\[5pt] &=24uv -2. \end{align*}

Finally, when $ \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1\\1 \end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

\[ \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(1,1)} = 24(1)(1) -2 = 22. \]

example.title: Evaluating a Jacobian Determinant

question.text:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix}\cos{u}\\\sin{v} \end{bmatrix} \]

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \pi/6\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) = \cos{u}$ and $y(u,v) = \sin{v}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &=-\sin{u} & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= 0\\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= 0 & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= \cos{v} \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} -\sin{u} & 0\\ 0 & \cos{v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (-\sin{u}) \cdot \cos{v} - 0 \cdot 0\\[5pt] &=-\sin{u} \cos v. \end{align*}

Finally, when $ \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \pi/6\\ 0 \end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

\[ \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{\left(\frac{\pi}6, 0\right)} =-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}6\right) \cos (0)= -\dfrac12. \]

question.text:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix}v^2+uv\\v-u \end{bmatrix} \]

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8\\-2 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) = v^2+uv$ and $y(u,v) = v-u.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &= v & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= 2v+u \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= -1 & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= 1 \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} v & 2v+u\\ -1& 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= v \cdot 1 - (2v+u) \cdot (-1) \\[5pt] &= v +2v+u \\[5pt] &= 3v+u. \end{align*}

Finally, when $ \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8\\-2 \end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

\[ \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(8,-2)} = 3(-2) +8= 2. \]

question.text:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} \cos(u+v)\\\sin(u-v) \end{bmatrix} \]

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} {\pi}/4\\ {\pi}/4\end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) =\cos(u+v)$ and $y(u,v) =\sin(u-v) .$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &= -\sin(u+v) & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= -\sin(u+v) \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= \cos(u-v) & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &=-\cos(u-v) \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} -\sin(u+v) & -\sin(u+v) \\ \cos(u-v) & - \cos(u-v) \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=(-\sin(u+v))\cdot (-\cos(u-v)) - (-\sin(u+v)) \cdot \cos(u-v) \\[5pt] &= \sin(u+v)\cos(u-v) + \sin(u+v)\cos(u-v) \\[5pt] &= 2\sin(u+v)\cos(u-v) . \end{align*}

Finally, when $ \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} {\pi}/4\\ {\pi}/4\end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

\[ \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{\left(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right)} = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\cos(0) = 2. \]

question.text:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} e^{u-v}\\ \ln(uv)\end{bmatrix}. \] compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $\begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1\\1 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Here, we have $x(u,v) = e^{u-v}$ and $y(u,v) = \ln(uv).$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &=e^{u-v} & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= -e^{u-v} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= \dfrac{1}{u} & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= \dfrac{1}{v} \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} e^{u-v} & -e^{u-v} \\ \dfrac{1}{u} & \dfrac{1}{v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=e^{u-v}\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{v}\right) - (-e^{u-v}) \cdot \dfrac{1}{u} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{u-v}}v+\dfrac{e^{u-v}}u. \end{align*}

Finally, when $ \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1\\1 \end{bmatrix},$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

\[ \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(1,1)} = \dfrac{e^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)}+\dfrac{e^{(1)-(1)}}{(1)} = 2. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation

question.text: Consider a small rectangle $\Delta$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(4,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta{A}.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by \[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{u}+v^2 \\ uv \end{bmatrix}? \]
question.explanation:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

\[ \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) \approx \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{Area}(\Delta)}_{\large \delta{A}} \]

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} & 2v \\ v & u \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} \cdot u - v \cdot 2v \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{u} - 2v^2 \\[10pt] \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(4,2)} &= \left.\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{u} - 2v^2 \, \right|_{u=4 \\ v=2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{4}- 2(2)^2 \\[5pt] &= -7 \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) &\approx |-7| \cdot \delta{A} \\[5pt] &= 7 \, \delta{A}. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider a small rectangle $\Delta$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(2,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta{A}.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by \[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{u}- v \\ u^2v \end{bmatrix}? \]
question.explanation:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

\[ \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) \approx \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{Area}(\Delta)}_{\large \delta{A}} \]

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{u^2} & -1 \\ 2uv & u^2 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \left(-\dfrac{1}{u^2}\right) \cdot (u^2) - 2uv \cdot (-1) \\[5pt] &=-1 + 2uv \\[10pt] \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(2,2)} &= (-1+2uv) \, \Big|_{u=2 \\ v=2} \\[5pt] &= -1+2(2)(2) \\[5pt] &= 7 \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) &\approx |7| \cdot \delta{A} \\[5pt] &= 7 \, \delta{A}. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider a small rectangle $\Delta$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(3,1)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta{A}.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by \[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} u^3-v \\ v-u \end{bmatrix}? \]
question.explanation:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

\[ \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) \approx \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{Area}(\Delta)}_{\large \delta{A}} \]

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} 3u^2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 3u^2 \cdot 1 - (-1) \cdot (-1) \\[5pt] &= 3u^2 - 1 \\[10pt] \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(3,1)} &= ( 3u^2 - 1 ) \, \Big|_{u=3 \\ v=1} \\[5pt] &= 3(3)^2 - 1 \\[5pt] &= 26 \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) &\approx |26| \cdot \delta{A} \\[5pt] &= 26 \, \delta{A}. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider a small rectangle $\Delta$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-1,1)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta{A}.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by \[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} ve^u \\ ue^v \end{bmatrix}? \]
question.explanation:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

\[ \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) \approx \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{Area}(\Delta)}_{\large \delta{A}} \]

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} ve^u & e^u \\ e^v & ue^v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= ve^u \cdot ue^v - e^v \cdot e^u \\[5pt] &= uve^{u+v} - e^{u+v} \\[5pt] &= (uv-1)e^{u+v}\\[10pt] \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(-1,1)} &= (uv-1)e^{u+v} \, \Big|_{u=-1 \\ v=1} \\[5pt] &= (-1\cdot 1-1)e^{-1+1}\\[5pt] &= -2 \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) &\approx |-2| \cdot \delta{A} \\[5pt] &= 2 \, \delta{A}. \end{align*}

example.title: Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation

question.text: Consider a small rectangle $\Delta$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-2,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta{A}.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by \[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} e^{u+v} \\ u^3+v \end{bmatrix}? \]
question.explanation:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

\[ \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) \approx \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{Area}(\Delta)}_{\large \delta{A}} \]

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} e^{u+v} & e^{u+v} \\ 3u^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= e^{u+v} \cdot 1 - 3u^2 \cdot e^{u+v} \\[5pt] &= e^{u+v}(1-3u^2) \\[10pt] \left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(-2,2)} &= e^{u+v}(1-3u^2) \, \Big|_{u=-2 \\ v=2} \\[5pt] &= e^{-2+2}(1-3(-2)^2) \\[5pt] &= -11 \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) &\approx |-11| \cdot \delta{A} \\[5pt] &= 11\, \delta{A}. \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by \[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} u^2+2v \\ -2u-v^2 \end{bmatrix}, \] is (locally) orientation-reversing?
question.explanation:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

\[ \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} < 0 \]

We have

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} u^2+2v \\ -2u-v^2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} 2u & 2 \\ -2 & -2v \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 2u \cdot (-2v) - (-2) \cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= -4uv + 4. \end{align*}

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

\begin{align*} %\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} &< 0 \\[5pt] -4uv +4 &< 0 \\[5pt] -4uv &< -4 \\[5pt] uv &> 1 \end{align*}

This gives the solution $v > \dfrac{1}{u}$ for $u>0$ and $v < \dfrac{1}{u}$ for $u< 0.$

Notice that the equation

\[ v=\dfrac{1}{u} \]

defines a hyperbola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,2)$ and $(-1,-2)$ satisfy the inequality.

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

question.explanation:

\[ \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} > 0. \]

\[ v=u \]
